asker_query: Madam, Ayesha-aapa has very bad pain — 8/10, can't sleep, can't eat. Family says morphine is haram, will cause nasha, she will not be able to say Kalima at the time of death. But she is suffering. How should I explain to the family? Should we still try?
answer:
It is deeply distressing to see Ayesha-aapa in such pain, but please reassure the family that managing severe pain is a compassionate, ethical, and medical priority.
According to the WHO Pain Ladder, her current medication (Step II: Tramadol) is insufficient for severe cancer pain.
Morphine (Step III) is the gold standard for severe pain; it is not "nasha" (addiction) when used for medical pain relief, nor does it hasten death or prevent a person from being conscious or spiritual.
It is a tool to relieve suffering so that the patient can find peace and comfort.
There is no standard upper dose limit for morphine in cancer pain; the correct dose is simply the amount required to make her pain-free with minimal side effects.
When starting morphine, you must always co-prescribe a laxative to prevent constipation and an anti-emetic (such as metoclopramide or domperidone) to prevent nausea.
As a caregiver, your role is to ensure the medication is given on time and to observe for side effects.
If the family remains hesitant, explain that untreated pain is a form of suffering that can be relieved, and that morphine is a medicine, not a sedative meant to cloud the mind.
If she experiences severe drowsiness, confusion, or muscle jerks (neurotoxicity), these are red flags that require immediate contact with her palliative care team to adjust the dosage.
Regular follow-up is essential to balance pain relief with side effects like constipation, dry mouth, or urinary retention.

_(The specific amount and schedule of any medicine are not included here. Take that part of your question to your next consultation.)_
